rows.text: Dispositions in the dark

Napoleon has deliberately given up the Pratzen plateau and left his right, along the lower Goldbach, looking thin enough to invite attack. Weyrother's Allied orders, read out at Krzenowitz after midnight to commanders who largely did not understand them, send four of five columns south-west across the French front. Fog fills the Goldbach valley. Soult's two assault divisions are standing in it, invisible from the heights.

rows.label: c. 01:00
rows.text: Weyrother reads the dispositions at Allied headquarters, Krzenowitz. Kutuzov reportedly dozes.

rows.label: c. 04:00
rows.text: The disposition orders the Allied columns to march at seven; Thiebault records reports through the night of the Allied left moving, judged by the noise. Liechtenstein's cavalry, misplaced on the left, must counter-march north across the front of the 4th Column; the Materialien has it ordered off only at dawn.

rows.label: before dawn
rows.text: Napoleon mounted at one in the morning to ride round his posts (the 30th Bulletin), and Thiebault has him on horseback long before day; the dispositions called his marshals to his bivouac for half past seven. His post, 'la butte' of the orders, is taken here to be the Zuran; the map places him there from 04:00, and the hour he took post is not established.
The Allied left opens the battle

Kienmayer's Austrian advance guard attacks Telnitz, the southernmost village on the Goldbach. Legrand's thin line holds the buildings and the vineyard bank above them, and the village changes hands repeatedly. Behind Kienmayer, Dokhturov's I Column is coming down off the southern end of the plateau.

rows.label: c. 07:00
rows.text: Kienmayer's advance guard attacks Telnitz. According to Stutterheim the musket fire there grew very murderous, and the Szekler infantry regiment lost two thirds of its men, dead and wounded.

rows.label: c. 07:00
rows.text: Dokhturov's I Column leaves its camp as the disposition ordered; Kutuzov's report has it force the enemy back to Telnitz about eight, and Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky has Dokhturov begin the attack on Telnitz at half past eight.

rows.label: c. 08:00
rows.text: Friant's leading brigade comes up to the Goldbach near Telnitz. The hour on the timeline is this map's: Stutterheim and the Moniteur's remarks of 1806 have Friant's men come up about nine, Schönhals has them attack about nine, Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky after Telnitz had fallen; Davout's report has word of the attack reach him on the march about eight and gives no hour for the brigade's arrival. The division had reached Raigern overnight: about 115 km from Vienna in under two days in Sokolov, thirty-six leagues in forty-eight hours in Thiers.

rows.text: Sokolnitz, the castle and the pheasantry

Langeron and Przybyszewski attack Sokolnitz village, its walled castle and the pheasantry enclosure beyond. Friant's leading brigade retakes Telnitz, then loses it again in the fog (Davout's report, which has the village in French hands at half past nine; the map shows it in this phase). On the plateau the 4th Column, which was meant to replace the troops leaving the heights, is still standing still: Liechtenstein's cavalry has cut across its line of march. A gap opens between it and the 3rd Column.

rows.label: c. 08:30

The hour is disputed: about eight in Ségur, the aide's report at half past eight in Thiebault, about nine in the Austrian accounts.

rows.text: Soult storms the heights

Saint-Hilaire and Vandamme climb out of the fog into sunlight onto a plateau the 4th Column is still crossing. St-Hilaire makes for the Pratzeberg south of Pratzen village, Vandamme for Stare Vinohrady, the 'old vineyards', north-east of the village. Kutuzov, riding with the 4th Column, sees the danger and begins pulling troops back. The Allied centre is being broken, but the plateau will not be firmly French until about 11:00.

rows.label: c. 08:45
rows.text: Soult's divisions advance. The mist lifts off the heights.

rows.label: c. 09:00
rows.text: Thiebault's brigade clears Pratzen village; the 10e Legere pushes on for the Pratzeberg.

rows.label: c. 09:15

The sun of Austerlitz, as memoirs call it
The crisis on the Pratzeberg

Kamensky's brigade, marching for Sokolnitz at the tail of Langeron's column, sees the French on the height behind it, turns about and attacks. Jurczek's Austrians join in and Saint-Hilaire is pushed back toward the crest. In the same hour, and independently, Lannes begins his advance astride the Olmutz highway in the north.

rows.label: c. 09:30
rows.text: Lannes advances along the highway. Bagration counter-attacks. The two battles now run in parallel.

rows.label: c. 09:45
rows.text: Kamensky turns his brigade about and drives the 10e Legere off the crest. No account read gives the hour of the turn, only its sequence; his brigade's record on this map puts it in the 08:45 phase.

rows.label: c. 10:15
rows.text: Jurczek's Austrians attack the Pratzeberg; French and Austrians briefly mistake each other's identity. No source read gives the hour; Schönhals makes the attack simultaneous with Kamensky's.

rows.label: c. 10:30
rows.text: Langeron rides back and sends reinforcements up the slope; they arrive as the position is lost. The Kursk regiment in the accounts that tell it, its loss disputed (up to 1,600 men in Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky; two battalions in Langeron's journal); the hour is this map's.

rows.text: The northern battle decided

Liechtenstein's and Uvarov's horse charge the French cavalry screen and Murat answers with Nansouty's and d'Hautpoul's cuirassiers. The Santon and its eighteen guns hold the flank, Blasowitz falls; in Thiers, Lannes then carries Holubitz and Krug and parts Bagration's infantry from Liechtenstein's cavalry, while in Schönhals Bagration's line is broken later, by Caffarelli's, Suchet's and d'Hautpoul's attacks. On the plateau, Saint-Hilaire's brigades carry their part of the Pratzen heights with their own charge, as Thiebault tells it, and Schönhals has Soult send Levasseur's brigade to support their right.

rows.label: c. 10:40
rows.text: The cavalry collision west of Blasowitz. Kellermann falls back through his infantry and reforms.

rows.label: c. 11:00
rows.text: The Pratzeberg is firmly in French hands.

rows.label: c. 11:15
rows.text: Blasowitz falls; no source read gives the hour, and the accounts differ on its order: the Allied report printed in 1806 has it fall before Liechtenstein sent in the uhlans, and Schönhals tells of it after the uhlans' charge, during the cavalry fights.
The Russian Guard at Stare Vinohrady

Grand Duke Constantine commits the Guard, which Stutterheim calls the reserve of the Allied right, against Vandamme on the Old Vineyards. In Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky the Guard infantry overthrows the first two French columns with the bayonet; in Schönhals the Life Guard Horse cuts down a battalion of the 4th Line and a light battalion of the 24th and takes the 4th's eagle, which an Allied official report, first printed in the Materialien of 1806, calls the only trophy of the day; who took it is disputed (the Life Guard Horse in Stutterheim and Schönhals, the Chevalier Guards in Marbot). Bessieres brings up the Guard cavalry and Rapp charges with the chasseurs and Mamelukes; a division of Bernadotte's corps, Drouet's by his own memoir as Sokolov quotes it, meets the attack, though Thiebault counts I Corps' 2nd division among the troops that took no part.

rows.label: c. 12:00
rows.text: Napoleon moves forward from the Zuran to Stare Vinohrady.

rows.label: c. 12:00
rows.text: Buxhowden, on the Allied left, is still unaware of the collapse behind him.

rows.label: c. 12:30
rows.text: Davout regroups and attacks; Langeron is forced back toward Sokolnitz.
The centre turns south

With the plateau secure and the Allied right pushed back beyond Blasowitz, Napoleon turns his centre ninety degrees. Saint-Hilaire and Vandamme come down off the heights onto the back of Buxhowden's three columns, supported by the Guard and the grenadier division, while Davout resumes the offensive from the west. Przybyszewski's column, caught between them in Sokolnitz, is surrounded.

rows.label: c. 13:00-14:00
rows.text: Soult and Davout launch the converging assault on the Allied left.

rows.label: c. 14:00
rows.text: Sokolnitz falls. Przybyszewski's column is broken up and largely captured.
Augezd, the ponds and the ice

By the afternoon a way out for the Allied left runs south over the defile at Augezd and the frozen meres beyond. This map reads it as a way left open, and the retreat the disposition ordered for the left, by the Turas wood, Kobelnitz and Puntowitz, as running through ground the French held. French guns on the heights fire down on the ice. The 30th Bulletin claimed twenty thousand Russians drowned here; Schönhals, on the Telnitz priest's word, has sixty to at most a hundred. General Suchet's report of 16 December 1805, as Sokolov quotes it, has thirty-six guns, 138 horses and three bodies taken from the pond near Augezd when it was drained; the figures usually given, thirty-eight guns, about a hundred and thirty horses and two men, were not traced to a source in this reading. Napoleon comes to the chapel of St Anthony above Augezd (Schönhals).

rows.text: The reckoning

The figures for the losses differ widely. Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky has the Russians lose up to 21,000 killed, wounded and taken and 133 guns, and the Austrians 5,922; Schönhals about 15,000 Russian prisoners and 5,000 to 6,000 killed and wounded; an unsigned official report, first printed in the Materialien of 1806, has 3,000 to 4,000 killed and wounded and 8,000 to 10,000 prisoners. Napoleon claimed forty colours on 3 December and forty-five on 5 December. The French reports, as Sokolov gives them, count 1,305 killed, 6,940 wounded and 573 taken or missing; Sokolov himself puts the French loss at nine to nine and a half thousand. Austria signs at Pressburg on 26 December. The Confederation of the Rhine follows in July, and on 6 August 1806 Francis II lays down the imperial crown, ending the Holy Roman Empire.

rows.text: No source read calls the corps the general reserve. The 30th Bulletin gives Bernadotte the command of the centre, with Rivaud's division on his left and Drouet's on his right (p. 449); Stutterheim (1806), an Austrian officer present at the battle, writes that the corps formed the centre of the French army (p. 41); Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky has Napoleon order Bernadotte and Soult together to seize the heights of Pratzen (1846, pp. 238-239); Marbot's memoirs have the centre formed by the troops of Soult and Bernadotte (vol. I, p. 260). Thiebault's memoirs count the 2nd division of I Corps, with the Guard and the reserve, among the troops that took no part in the fighting (vol. III, p. 466; the reserve is the grenadiers' on p. 504, in a boast he imputes to Napoleon). A note in the Materialien of 1806, by its lettering one of an unnamed French officer's (an attribution read on the text layer only), has half of the corps' battalions fire no cartridge and the other half take little part (p. 93); Savary has one of its divisions break the Russian Guard's infantry (1828, pp. 205-208).

This map reads the Bulletin's figure as propaganda and the catastrophe as encirclement rather than drowning: an interpretation.

Positions here are reconstructed from standard accounts of the battle. Village-level locations and the sequence of attacks follow the accounts; the hours are partly dated in the sources read, partly disputed between them, and mostly this map's own, as each move's timing grade, and each event's timing and dispute, say. Exact frontages, the spacing between formations and the precise placement of cavalry reserves are not — a Napoleonic corps occupied a shifting area of ground, not a point.

Every formation marker therefore carries a confidence grade. A means the position is documented; B means the sector is documented but the frontage shown is an approximation; C means the position is reconstructed from the narrative and should be treated as indicative only.

Strengths are the hardest figures of all. The Allied column organisation split and intermingled regiments, and reputable orders of battle disagree substantially — Dokhturov's I Column is given as anything from 7,750 to 14,200 men. Where sources conflict, the dossier shows a working figure and the range.

Terrain relief is exaggerated about {EXAG} times: one map unit is {M_PER_UNIT} m on the ground, and heights follow a separate vertical scale fitted to surveyed elevations. At true scale the Pratzen plateau reads as a gentle rise, about 115 m from the Goldbach to the Pratzeberg over some 2.5 km. The relief setting cannot be changed while the battle plays, because redrawing the ground can take longer than a frame; the ground switch (Landscape, Paper map, Landscape with counters) can, and a slow frame while it redraws advances the battle clock by at most 1.2 minutes at 1× (4.8 at four times speed).

Villages are placed from the Czech municipality register, Turas, which it does not list, at the Czech address register's point for Tuřany, the name Wolny's topography of 1836 gives it, and summits from terrain-model data; the map keeps its historical frame, which lies about {ROT} degrees off true north. The compass rose shows true north for the current view. Raigern, Rausnitz and Kowalowitz lie beyond the frame and are shown as markers at its edge.

Open questions, left unresolved rather than guessed: the pattern of Russian infantry flags; whether Grenz infantry wore brown in 1805; whether vines stood at Telnitz and at Stare Vinohrady in 1805; the upper bound of the Russian Guard's attack; Bagration's exact line at dawn; the exact place of the Posoritz post house; the positions of Krug and Bellowitz, which no source read fixes; Kologrivov's command on 2 December, which rests on Sokolov alone (Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky and the Chevalier Guard's history have him command the Guard cavalry at Olmütz and on the march, and the Chevalier Guard came up in Maliutin's separate column); when Blasowitz fell; when Napoleon took post on the Zuran; when Bernadotte's corps, Drouet's division with it, crossed the Goldbach; how many guns stood by the chapel of St Anthony, and whose; how many men drowned in the meres; how Suchet's and Caffarelli's divisions were numbered on the day (Suchet's the 3rd of V Corps in both October returns read, Gazan's the 2nd on 26 October; Caffarelli's, under Bisson on 28 October, the 1st of III Corps); the brigade of Gladkov cited from Duffy and Smith, which no source read names; whether Uvarov's regiments were with Liechtenstein's column or had gone to Bagration the evening before; the numbers of Rivaud's and Drouet's divisions in I Corps, which the October returns give differently; and the hours on which the accounts read disagree with each other or with this map's timing: when the columns left the plateau (at 07:00 as the disposition ordered, the I Column at seven in Buxhowden's and Kutuzov's reports and so on the map, half past six for the left wing in Schönhals, between seven and eight in Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky; the II and III Columns at 07:30 in Schönhals, the III at 07:00 in Przybyszewski's report and the II coming down at 08:00 in Buxhowden's; all three from 07:00 on the map), when Kamensky turned his brigade about (no account read gives the hour; at 09:45 in the event, in the 08:45 phase in his brigade's record), when Rapp's counter-charge went in (by about noon in Schönhals, before one by the order of the Bulletin's narrative, about 13:00 in Rapp's and Ségur's memoirs; from 11:15 on the map), when Friant's division left Raigern (at 05:00, or between 05:30 and 06:00, in Davout's two reports, about 06:00 in Sokolov; from 04:00 on the map), when its leading brigade reached the Goldbach (about 09:00 in Stutterheim and the Moniteur's remarks of 1806; 08:00 on the map), when it retook Telnitz (in French hands at 09:30 in Davout's report, then lost again; 08:30 on the map), and when Bagration's corps fell back (with Blasowitz's fall on the map, 11:15; after an attack on its left toward noon in Schönhals). The map keeps its timing for Kamensky's turn, Rapp's charge, Friant's division and Bagration's corps. Duffy (1977) and Smith (1998), cited here for strengths, were not read. Kamensky's musketeer regiment is named here as Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky names it, Ryazhsk; the Materialien of 1806 give Ryazan, as this map earlier cited from Duffy, which is kept as the other reading. Two known limits of the terrain model are left as they are rather than reshaped to fit: its stream beds are not downhill at every point (reverse gradients of up to about 10 m within a reach), and from the chapel of St Anthony it does not show the centre of the Satschan pond, although Lejeune has Napoleon at the end on a knoll above Augezd facing the lakes, which this map takes to be the chapel's height.

Two figures on the situation line are computed from the plotted reconstruction rather than taken from a source. The holding on the heights is the sum of the strengths of formations whose plotted positions fall inside the plateau outline; because the reconstruction plots formations and not losses, a figure that does not change does not mean the fighting there has stopped. Centre separation is a spatial test, not a historical statistic: it reports whether a French formation stands across the line joining the Allied groups north and south of the plateau. When it stops being reported the geometry no longer holds, which is not the same as the Allied army having reunited.

rows.label: Historical record
rows.text: What the sources attest: who was there, roughly how many, which villages were attacked and when. Marked as fact in an event's dossier.

rows.label: Reconstruction
rows.text: How this map represents the record: a plotted position, a route between anchors, a frontage. Graded A, B or C for confidence; a formation's dossier names the grade as its position's: documented, estimated or reconstructed.

rows.label: Derived reading
rows.text: What the engine computes from the plot, such as the holding on the heights or the centre-separation test. Never a source figure; the holding on the heights and the centre-separation test are marked derived wherever they are shown.

Order-of-battle figures are this map's working figures, many first taken from Duffy (1977) and Smith (1998), cited and not read; where a formation's note names a source or gives what the sources read, it says so, and a figure without a note is this map's.

Narrative of the fight for the Pratzeberg draws on Thiebault's memoirs, with Schönhals and Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky where the statements name them; Duffy (1977), on which it earlier drew, was not read.

Figures for the meres: General Suchet's report of 16 December 1805, as Sokolov quotes it (2006, t. II, pp. 70-71, his note 88 citing Alombert and Colin, Paris, 2002, t. 5, p. 297; the French text was not read), has the pond near Augezd drained over five days and 36 Russian guns, 138 horse carcasses and three bodies taken from it; the figures usually given, 38 guns, about 130 horses and two men, were not traced to a source in this reading.

Soult's 'twenty minutes at most' and Napoleon's further quarter of an hour are a memoir anecdote, told here as Thiebault's memoirs tell it (vol. III, 1894, pp. 456-458), who sets it 'au jour naissant' and has the signal follow an aide's report at half past eight (p. 504); Ségur tells the same exchange with ten minutes and has the divisions appear at eight (vol. II, 1877, p. 466); Savary has Napoleon hold the marshals until the attack on his right had become serious. The hour this map gives it is its own.

Marbot's and Thiebault's memoirs tell of thousands drowned when the Guard's guns broke the ice of the Satschan mere (Marbot, vol. I, pp. 262-263, in the 27th edition read, first published 1891; Thiebault, vol. III, 1894, p. 466, three to four thousand), and Lejeune of more than six thousand (1895, vol. I, pp. 39-40); Stutterheim has some die (1806, pp. 74-75), and the editor of the Materialien prefers his word to the Bulletin's twenty thousand (1806, p. 121); Schönhals, on the Telnitz priest's statement, has sixty to at most a hundred and calls the mass drowning a French exaggeration (1873, pp. 169-170); all against the count from the drained pond.

rows.text: 'The sun of Austerlitz' is a phrase the memoirs use: Thiebault puts it in quotation marks for the rising sun, which in his telling greets the attack on Telnitz and Sokolnitz and then lights the climb onto the Pratzen (vol. III, 1894, p. 461); Marbot has it appear in all its brilliance as the centre climbs toward Pratzen, and calls it the sun Napoleon so liked to recall (vol. I, p. 260, the 27th edition); neither gives that climb a clock hour. Participants put daybreak or the sun about eight (Thiebault: 'le jour ne venait qu'à huit heures'; Lejeune: 'il était huit heures du matin lorsque le soleil se leva'); this map computes its sun and takes no hour from them.

Weyrother's dispositions send four of the five Allied columns south-west off the Pratzen plateau to turn the French right and cut the road to Vienna. Bagration holds the highway in the north, Liechtenstein's cavalry links the two, and the Russian Guard stands in reserve behind Krzenowitz. The plan assumes the French will stand still while those four columns march across their front.

Napoleon abandoned the Pratzen plateau on 1 December and camped his army west of it, behind the Goldbach. He asked for an armistice interview and let his outposts be pushed in. His proclamation to the army that day says in terms that the enemy, marching to turn his right, will present its flank; the 30th Bulletin says everything tended to confirm the Russian general in his ill-calculated operation, and Marbot calls the thin right a trap. This map reads the thinness of the right as meant to draw the Allies off the high ground in the centre.

Legrand's single division held roughly five kilometres of the lower Goldbach on its own. Davout's III Corps detachment, some 4,300 men by Duffy's and Smith's count, reached Raigern only on the night of 1 December after a forced march from Vienna, 8 km from the villages it had to hold. Against them the Allies committed roughly 33,000 to 40,000. The weakness was real, not simulated, which is what made it convincing.

Between 07:00 and 09:00 the three left-hand columns and Kienmayer's advance guard descended into the Goldbach villages and fed themselves into the fight for them. Each column that went down was a column no longer on the plateau. This map reads the Allies as having thinned the centre of their position themselves by the time Soult moved; Stutterheim and Thiebault have the 4th Column still on the plateau when the French appeared.

Saint-Hilaire and Vandamme had been standing in fog in the Goldbach valley, invisible from the heights. At about 08:45 they climbed the western slope and struck the 4th Column, which was still on the plateau. The disposition set every column off at seven; Stutterheim has the 4th Column ordered off only toward eight, to give the left wing's columns time, and Schönhals has it leave half an hour after the first three; Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky has it held up by Liechtenstein's cavalry crossing its line of march and then by Kutuzov standing still, though the disposition ordered him forward. The fight for the two summits lasted about two hours in Stutterheim and Schönhals, three in Thiebault; on this map the plateau is French from end to end by about 11:00.

rows.text: With the plateau taken, the Allied army was in two halves that could no longer support one another. Buxhowden's columns, roughly 33,000 to 40,000 men, were west and south of the heights; Bagration and the Guard were north and east of them. Buxhowden did not learn that the centre had gone until about noon. From this point the French hold the interior lines on their enemy's own battlefield.

Grand Duke Constantine threw the Guard, which Stutterheim calls the reserve of the Allied right, at Vandamme on the Old Vineyards. In Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky the Guard infantry overthrew the first two French columns with the bayonet; in Schönhals the Life Guard Horse cut down a battalion of the 4th Line and a light battalion of the 24th and took the 4th's eagle, which an Allied official report, first printed in the Materialien of 1806, calls the only trophy of the day; who took it is disputed (the Life Guard Horse in Stutterheim and Schönhals, the Chevalier Guards in Marbot). Bessieres brought up the Guard cavalry and Rapp charged with the chasseurs and Mamelukes; a division of Bernadotte's corps, Drouet's by his own memoir as Sokolov quotes it, met the attack, though Thiebault counts I Corps' 2nd division among the troops that took no part. Prince Repnin was taken prisoner.

rows.text: The northern battle was a holding action that Lannes turned into an advance. This map reads the Santon, scarped and carrying eighteen guns, as anchoring the flank, so that Bagration could not get past it. When Liechtenstein's and Uvarov's horse charged, Murat answered with Nansouty's and d'Hautpoul's cuirassiers. Blasowitz fell, about 11:15 by this map's reckoning (no source read gives the hour); in Thiers, Lannes then carries Holubitz and Krug and parts Bagration's infantry from Liechtenstein's cavalry, while Schönhals has Bagration's battalions thrown into disorder after an attack on his left toward noon, when the Guards had given way, then gathered again, somewhat, on the height by Rausnitz.

Between about 13:00 and 14:00 Napoleon turned his centre ninety degrees and brought it down off the plateau onto the back of Buxhowden's columns, while Davout attacked from the west. Przybyszewski's column was surrounded in Sokolnitz and largely captured. The Allied left was now being attacked from the direction of its own rear.

This map reads a way left to the Allied left as the neck of dry ground at Augezd between the two meres, with French guns on the height above it, and the retreat the disposition had ordered for the left, by the Turas wood, Kobelnitz and Puntowitz, as running through ground the French held. Some formations broke south across the frozen water. The 30th Bulletin claimed twenty thousand drowned; General Suchet's report of 16 December 1805, as Sokolov quotes it, has thirty-six guns, 138 horses and three bodies taken from the pond near Augezd when it was drained, and the figures usually given, thirty-eight guns, about a hundred and thirty horses and two men, were not traced to a source in this reading. The catastrophe was real; this map reads it as encirclement rather than drowning, an interpretation.

rows.text: A retreat of the left. No order of the day naming its route has been read (the disposition's retreat for the left ran by the Turas wood, Kobelnitz and Puntowitz); that it went south over the Augezd defile and the meres is inferred from the accounts of the end (Schönhals).

rows.text: That the way out by Augezd came under artillery fire from the height (Schönhals's 'auf der Höhe'; that it is the height above Augezd, ground the army had held at dawn, is this map's reading); what the command knew of it is inferred.
Drafted by Gen. Franz von Weyrother, Quartermaster-General. Read aloud at Krzenowitz after midnight, in German, to an audience largely of Russian officers, with no time to copy it out.

Turn the French right with overwhelming weight, force the Goldbach at the southern villages, then wheel the left wing north-west to envelop the French as they fall back toward Brünn - severing their line to Vienna - and roll them up against the hills. The centre is to follow the attack, not hold the plateau.
That the French were retreating and would not stand.
That the Pratzen plateau could safely be vacated because the decisive ground was the French right.
That five columns could cross one another's lines of march in darkness and arrive in order.

All three assumptions were wrong. Execution compounded them: the 4th Column, ordered off only toward eight in Stutterheim and leaving half an hour after the first three in Schönhals, was held up by the cavalry column's counter-march and then by Kutuzov standing still (Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky), and was still on the plateau when Soult arrived.

rows.text: Precede the 1st Column, seize Telnitz at first light, then screen the outer flank toward Menitz.
Descend from the southern plateau, force the crossing at Telnitz, then wheel north-west toward the Turas wood (the disposition's name for it).
Take Sokolnitz, cross the stream, conform on Dokhturov's right.
Take the Sokolnitz castle and the pheasantry, cross, and link the attack to the centre.
Move from Pratzen to Kobelnitz and hold the hinge between the attack and the right.
Cavalry. Cover the right of the attacking columns between Blasowitz and the plateau.
Hold the Olmutz highway, pin the French left, and link to Liechtenstein.
The Imperial Guard to remain behind Krzenowitz, in hand.

Set out in the proclamation to the army and the orders of 1 December, and in the written dispositions of that evening, which placed Soult's three divisions beyond the ravine at seven and called the marshals to his bivouac for the morning. The moment of the last orders differs: at the first rays of the sun in the 30th Bulletin; in Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky once the sun lit the hilltops, the marshals having been summoned to the barrow by Schlapanitz before dawn; in Savary only once the attack on the right was pronounced.

rows.text: Invite the attack on the right by giving up the Pratzen plateau and holding the lower Goldbach thin. When the enemy centre has marched off the heights to join that attack, take the heights with two divisions held concealed in the valley, cut the Allied army in half, then wheel south onto the rear of everything that has gone down into the Goldbach. In Ségur and Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky Bernadotte is to assail the plateau from the left at the same time; the written dispositions do not say so: they put I Corps onto Caffarelli's ground of the day before, its left behind the Santon, in column until new orders.
That the Allies would read the abandoned plateau and the withdrawn outposts as weakness.
That Davout could reach the lower Goldbach from Vienna in time to keep the right alive.
That Legrand could hold roughly five kilometres of stream on his own for several hours.

The risk was carried entirely on the right. In this map's interpretation, a counterfactual: if Davout had not arrived, or if Legrand had broken before nine o'clock, the bait would have been swallowed with the army behind it.
Hold the villages on the lower Goldbach and give ground slowly. Do nothing that might discourage the attack.
Saint-Hilaire behind Puntowitz, Vandamme behind Girzikowitz, out of sight in the valley. On the signal, take the Pratzeberg and Stare Vinohrady.
Climb the northern shoulder of the plateau and take the Old Vineyards, linking the assault to Lannes.
Hold the Olmutz highway with the Santon fortified and entrenched. Advance only when the centre has gone in.
The Guard and the grenadiers the reserve with the Emperor (the 30th Bulletin), the grenadiers under Lannes's orders in the dispositions of 1 December. The route drawn is this map's.
Once the plateau is held from Pratzen to the highway, turn the centre ninety degrees and come down on the rear of the Allied left.
Napoleon has given up the plateau and left his right thin. The Allies form to attack it.
Four columns go down into the Goldbach villages. The centre of the Allied position empties behind them.
Soult climbs out of the fog onto ground the Allies have just left, and holds it against everything sent back.
With the plateau lost the Allied army is in two halves. The Guard, which Stutterheim calls the reserve of the Allied right, attacks to take it back and is thrown back.
The French centre turns south onto the rear of an Allied left that is still attacking westward.
The Allied columns begin to leave the plateau
Every column that goes down into the valley is a column no longer holding the centre.

When the columns left the plateau: the disposition ordered all the columns to march at 07:00, and the I Column left its camp at seven (Buxhowden's and Kutuzov's reports), as did the III Column in Przybyszewski's report; Schönhals has the left wing off at half past six and the II and III Columns at 07:30, Buxhowden's report the II Column coming down at 08:00, and Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky the first three columns between seven and eight. The map moves the three columns from 07:00, the disposition's hour.

The cavalry column had been posted on the wrong flank overnight; in Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky its crossing of the line of march held up the 4th Column at the set hour, and Kutuzov then stood still, though the disposition ordered him forward. Stutterheim has the 4th Column ordered off only toward eight, to give the left wing's columns time, and Schönhals has it leave half an hour after the first three.

rows.text: Kienmayer attacks Telnitz
The battle opens here, on the Allied left, after a night of outpost contact along the Goldbach: the beginning of the attack Napoleon wanted.
Friant's division at Raigern since the night

Davout and Friant reached Raigern on the night of 1 December: about 115 km from Vienna in under two days in Sokolov, thirty-six leagues in forty-eight hours in Thiers. Davout's reports send the division on from Raigern at 05:00 (his report of 2 December) or between 05:30 and 06:00 (his report of 26 December), Sokolov about six; this map moves it from 04:00. Raigern lies just beyond this corner of the map.

rows.text: Napoleon releases Soult against the heights

Asked how long his troops needed to crown the plateau, Soult is reported to have answered twenty minutes at most (Thiebault) or ten (Ségur), and Napoleon to have waited a further quarter of an hour, giving the signal only once an aide reported the heights abandoned (a little prematurely, Thiebault adds). A memoir anecdote. The hour is disputed: about eight in Ségur, the aide's report at half past eight in Thiebault, the French columns moving about nine in the Austrian accounts.

rows.text: Saint-Hilaire and Vandamme climb the slope
Two divisions that had been standing in fog, invisible from the crest, climb onto a plateau the 4th Column has not yet left (Stutterheim; Schönhals; Thiebault).
Thiebault's brigade clears Pratzen village

Opens the way to the Pratzeberg. No source read gives its hour: the Allied accounts have the 4th Column's advance guard occupy the village as the French moved off, and Thiebault expected only posts there.
Kutuzov orders the 4th Column to face about
The Allied commander-in-chief, riding with the column, sees what has happened.
Kamensky turns his brigade about and drives the French off the crest

Allied initiative on the plateau, but whose is disputed: Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky, citing Langeron's report, has Kamensky see the French climbing, warn Langeron and turn his brigade against them; Schönhals has Langeron send the brigade; Kutuzov's official report has Kutuzov order Kamensky to occupy the ridge, and Stutterheim has the two regiments come on the commander-in-chief's order; Kutuzov's private relation of March 1806 has them turn from the column and names no order of his.

rows.text: When Kamensky turned his brigade about: no account read gives the hour, only a sequence, after the French began to climb the heights and before or with Jurczek's attack. This event puts the turn at 09:45; his brigade's record on this map turns it in the 08:45 phase, whose timing the map keeps.
Langeron's reinforcements arrive as the crest is lost

Langeron rode back and sent troops up toward Kamensky. The accounts name the Kursk regiment: Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky has Langeron bring it up too late, losing up to 1,600 men; Langeron's journal, as Sokolov quotes it, two of its battalions, half killed and half taken with their guns and colours; Schönhals has it left in reserve behind Sokolnitz and mostly taken there. rows.text: The Pratzeberg is firmly in French hands
From here the French centre holds the high ground above the Goldbach valley and, in time, comes down into the back of the Allied columns fighting in it.
The French take Blasowitz from the Russian Guard

The Russian Guard's jägers held the village in Stutterheim, Schönhals and Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky; the Chevalier Guard's history instead has the French occupy it without hindrance. Its attackers are disputed: Bernadotte's corps, Rivaud on the left and Drouet on the right, in Stutterheim; the 1st division of Lannes's V Corps in Thiebault; part of Rivaud's division ordered onto it with Caffarelli and Kellermann in Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky; Caffarelli's 13e Legere in Sokolov; Marbot has Lannes throw the Russians back from the Santon as far as Blasowitz. Bagration's separation is a later action: Schönhals has his battalions thrown into disorder after an attack on his left toward noon, when the Guards had given way, then gathered again, somewhat, on the height by Rausnitz.

rows.text: The Russian Guard takes the eagle of the 4th Line

The Guard, which Stutterheim calls the reserve of the Allied right, takes the eagle of the 4th Line, which an Allied official report, first printed in the Materialien of 1806, calls the only trophy of the day. The hour is disputed: Rapp and Ségur put the Guard's last effort about 13:00, Schönhals has the fight over by about noon; the window is this map's.
Rapp's counter-charge breaks the Chevalier Guard
Prince Repnin is taken prisoner, by Rapp's charge in the 30th Bulletin. With the reserve spent, nothing remains to retake the plateau.

When Rapp's charge went in: before one by the order of the narrative in the 30th Bulletin and in Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky (an inference: neither dates the charge itself), by about noon in Schönhals, about 13:00 or after in Rapp's own memoirs and Ségur's; the map draws it from 11:15, a timing it has kept.

rows.text: Napoleon moves forward to Stare Vinohrady

From Stare Vinohrady he directs the centre while the Allied left is still fighting westward on the Goldbach with its rear open. Later he moves again, to the chapel of St Anthony above Augezd (Schönhals); Lejeune has him at the end on a knoll above Augezd facing the lakes, which this map takes to be the chapel's height.
Buxhowden does not yet know the centre is gone
Contemporaries put it about noon. Three columns go on attacking westward while the army behind them is being taken apart.
Davout resumes the offensive
The anvil becomes a hammer. Langeron is pushed back onto Sokolnitz from the west.
The French centre turns south
Ninety degrees, off the heights, into the rear of Buxhowden's three columns.
Sokolnitz falls; Przybyszewski's column is surrounded
The column tries to break out toward Kobelnitz, comes apart, and surrenders almost entire.
Vandamme takes the height above the Augezd defile

A way out for the Allied left over the Augezd defile now lies under French guns; this map reads the retreat the disposition ordered for the left, by the Turas wood, Kobelnitz and Puntowitz, as running through ground the French held.
French artillery fires on the ice of the Satschan mere

The 30th Bulletin claimed twenty thousand drowned; Schönhals calls the mass drowning a French exaggeration and, on the Telnitz priest's word, puts it at sixty to at most a hundred. General Suchet's report of 16 December 1805, as Sokolov quotes it, has thirty-six guns, 138 horses and three bodies taken from the pond near Augezd when it was drained, by inference a lower bound, not the toll; the figures usually given, thirty-eight guns, about a hundred and thirty horses and two men, were not traced to a source in this reading. This map reads the catastrophe as encirclement rather than drowning, an interpretation.

rows.text: Organised resistance ends
Bagration holds the height toward Rausnitz, then withdraws on Austerlitz, the Guard on Austerlitz, and the Allied left has ceased to exist as a formation.

When the fighting ended: this map puts the end of organised resistance at 16:30, after Sokolov's end of the firing in the north; an Allied report printed in 1806 has the northern front quiet from 15:00, Thiebault the firing over about half an hour after three, and Mikhailovsky-Danilevsky the last shots between five and six; the 30th Bulletin has the victory decided at one. Schönhals has Bagration, no longer attacked, retreat on Austerlitz about 18:00, and Stutterheim behind Austerlitz at 18:00.

rows.text: Ten kilometres of open Moravian farmland. The French army, marked in blue, is to the west; to the east are the Russians and the Austrians, marked in amber. Between them runs the Goldbach, a small stream in a marshy bottom, and behind it stands the Pratzen plateau, the high ground in the centre of the field.

Weyrother's orders send four of the five Allied columns south-west, off the plateau, to turn the French right and cut the road to Vienna. The heavy arrows are the intended lines of march. Note what they all have in common: they lead away from the centre.

Napoleon gave up the plateau on 1 December and camped behind the Goldbach, leaving his right so thin that a single division held five kilometres of stream. The weakness was real, which is what made it convincing.

From seven o'clock the Allied left goes down into the villages and stays there. Watch the figure on the plateau outline, a reading derived from the plotted positions with every man counted once: the Allied strength on the heights falls from about 39,000 at 04:00 to about 19,000 by 07:25, half of it gone before a shot is fired at the plateau.

In this model's terrain an observer on the Pratzeberg summit can see about 73 per cent of the field, and one on the valley floor at Puntowitz under 3 per cent. That is a reading from the model, not a record of what anyone saw: on the morning of the battle the valley lay in fog, and it was the fog that hid Soult's divisions forming at the foot of the slope.
At about a quarter to nine Saint-Hilaire and Vandamme climb out of the fog onto a plateau the Allies are leaving. Two divisions, the Guard held back, against a column still filing off the heights.

With the plateau gone the Allied army is in two halves that can no longer help one another. Buxhowden's columns are still attacking westward and will not learn what has happened behind them until about noon.

The French centre turns ninety degrees and comes down off the heights into the rear of the Allied left. A way out for them is the neck of dry ground at Augezd, under guns on ground the Allies held at dawn.

The accounts put the Allied losses anywhere from about eleven thousand to more than twenty-five thousand killed, wounded and taken; the French reports count near nine thousand. Everything you have watched today is a reconstruction: positions are graded A, B or C, strengths carry their ranges, and two figures on the situation line are computed rather than recorded. The sources panel says which is which.
